title: Doenjang jjigae (soybean paste stew)
blurb: Everyday Korean soybean paste stew: potato, courgette, mushroom and tofu in anchovy dashi. Mild, savoury, 30 minutes.
intro: The everyday stew that comes with rice at a Korean table: deeply savoury from fermented soybean paste, not spicy unless you add the chilli. Cooked in a wide steel sauté pan with a lid (26–28 cm, sides 5 cm or more) instead of a clay pot. Stainless steel is fine with salty, fermented food. The lid stays on for most of the cooking because a wide pan loses liquid quickly. Use niboshi dashi if you have it. Shrimp, clams or cubes of beef are optional; vegetables and tofu alone make a complete stew. This is a home adaptation built from several Korean sources and has not been kitchen tested.
equipment: Wide steel sauté pan with lid, 26–28 cm

mise.name: Potato and onion
mise.items: potato in 1.5 cm cubes · onion in 2 cm squares

mise.name: Courgette, mushrooms, garlic
mise.items: courgette in 1 cm half-moons · mushrooms torn or quartered · garlic minced

mise.name: Tofu and protein
mise.items: tofu in 2 cm cubes · shrimp or clams, if using

mise.name: Finish
mise.items: spring onion in 3 cm lengths · green pepper sliced on the diagonal

steps.title: Cut everything to size
body: Peel the potato and cut it into 1.5 cm cubes. Cut the onion into 2 cm squares.
Halve the courgette lengthwise and cut it into 1 cm half-moons. Tear oyster mushrooms into strips or quarter button mushrooms. Mince the garlic.
Cut the tofu into 2 cm cubes. Cut the spring onion into 3 cm lengths and slice the green pepper on the diagonal.
If using beef, cut it into 1.5 cm cubes, no thin slicing needed.

steps.title: Dissolve the paste; simmer the potato
body: If using beef: heat the oil in the pan on medium-high and brown the cubes for 2–3 minutes.

Pour the dashi into the pan and bring it to a boil. Hold a small sieve or ladle in the dashi, put the doenjang (and gochujang, if using) in it and press it through with a spoon until no lumps are left.
Add the potato and onion. Cover and simmer on medium for 6 minutes.

steps.title: Add courgette and mushrooms
body: Add the courgette, mushrooms and garlic. Cover again and simmer for 4 minutes, until the courgette is just tender at the edges.
The liquid should still cover most of the vegetables. A wide pan loses liquid quickly, so top up with a splash of hot water if it has dropped below half.

steps.title: Tofu and shrimp or clams; taste
body: Slide in the tofu and the shrimp or clams. Simmer uncovered for 2–3 minutes, until the shrimp turn pink or the clams open. Throw away any clams that stay shut.
Taste the broth. Too mild: press in another teaspoon of doenjang. Too salty: add a little hot water. Sprinkle in the gochugaru now if you want gentle warmth.

steps.title: Finish and serve from the pan
body: Scatter the spring onion and green pepper over the top and simmer for 30 seconds.
Bring the pan to the table on a trivet and eat with plain rice. Spoon the stew over the rice or eat it alongside.

notes: Why a steel pan works

A jjigae is a shallow stew, so a wide pan with high sides does the job of a clay pot. The difference is evaporation: keep the lid on until the tofu goes in, and keep a cup of hot water nearby. Stainless steel is fine with fermented paste. A carbon-steel pan would lose its seasoning.
Doenjang brands vary

Saltiness differs a lot between brands, so start at 2½ tbsp and add more at the end. Doenjang is the brown Korean paste. Japanese miso works in a pinch but tastes sweeter and milder; use a little more and add ½ tsp soy sauce.
No dashi?
Simmer 6 dried anchovies (heads and guts removed) and a 5 cm piece of kombu in 750 ml water for 10 minutes, then lift them out. Plain water with an extra spoon of doenjang also works.

title: Andong jjimdak (soy-braised chicken)
blurb: Bone-in chicken braised in sweet soy with potato, carrot and glass noodles that soak up the sauce. Savoury, not spicy.
intro: A braise from the city of Andong: chicken on the bone in a glossy soy, garlic and brown sugar sauce, with chunks of potato and carrot and chewy glass noodles stirred in at the end. Traditionally it has a few dried chillies for warmth. Here they are optional, so it is savoury-sweet rather than hot. A wide steel sauté pan with a lid (28 cm) is ideal. Brown the chicken skin-side down first, then braise covered and reduce uncovered so the sauce coats everything. Use ordinary chicken pieces; nothing needs thin slicing. This is a home adaptation built from several Korean sources and has not been kitchen tested.
equipment: Wide steel sauté pan with lid, 28 cm

mise.name: Soaking
mise.items: glass noodles in warm water · dried shiitake in warm water

mise.name: Braising sauce
mise.items: soy · brown sugar · oyster sauce · garlic · ginger · pepper

mise.name: Onion and spring onion
mise.items: onion in thick lengthwise wedges · spring onion in 4 cm lengths

steps.title: Soak the noodles; cut the vegetables
body: Cover the glass noodles with warm water and soak for 30 minutes. Soak the dried shiitake in a separate cup of warm water.
Pat the chicken dry. If the drumsticks or thighs are very large, ask the butcher to chop them in half through the bone, or leave them whole.

Peel the potatoes and carrot and cut them into large 4 cm chunks; they braise for a long time and must not fall apart. Cut the onion through the root into thick lengthwise wedges. Cut the spring onions into 4 cm lengths.
Mix the soy sauce, brown sugar, oyster sauce, minced garlic, ginger and pepper into the braising sauce.

steps.title: Brown the chicken skin-side down
body: Heat the oil in the steel pan on medium-high until it shimmers. Lay the chicken in skin-side down in one layer and leave it alone for 6–8 minutes, until the skin is golden and releases from the pan by itself.
Turn the pieces and brown the other side for 2 minutes. Tip out all but about 1 tbsp of the rendered fat. The brown film on the pan is flavour; keep it.

steps.title: Add sauce and water; braise covered
body: Pour in the braising sauce and the water. Scrape the bottom of the pan with a wooden spatula so the brown film dissolves into the liquid. Add the dried chillies, if using.
Bring to a boil, cover, then lower to medium-low and braise for 15 minutes. Turn the pieces once halfway.

steps.title: Add potato, carrot and mushrooms
body: Squeeze the shiitake, remove the stems and halve the caps. Tuck the potato, carrot and shiitake between the chicken pieces so they sit in the liquid.
Cover and braise for 12–15 minutes, until a knife slides into the potato with little resistance.

steps.title: Uncover and reduce to a glossy sauce
body: Take off the lid and add the onion and the white parts of the spring onion. Raise the heat to medium and simmer for 5 minutes. Spoon the sauce over the chicken as it thickens.
Stop when about 2 cm of sauce is left: the noodles still need some to absorb. If it is already shallow, add 100 ml water.

steps.title: Fold in the noodles and finish
body: Drain the noodles and lay them in the sauce around the chicken. Turn them gently with tongs for 3–4 minutes, until they turn clear, soft and brown from the sauce.
Turn off the heat. Drizzle with sesame oil and scatter the green parts of the spring onion and the sesame seeds. Serve from the pan with rice.

notes: Glass noodles

Korean dangmyeon are grey, made from sweet potato starch, and stay chewy. Thin mung bean vermicelli works too: soak it only 10 minutes and simmer only 1–2 minutes, because it softens fast. The noodles keep drinking sauce after you turn off the heat, so serve straight away.
Boneless thighs
Use 700 g boneless skinless thighs cut into 5 cm chunks. Brown them for 3–4 minutes, braise for only 8 minutes before adding the potato, and use 400 ml water.
A little heat
Two whole dried chillies give gentle warmth without making it spicy. For more heat, crack them open, or add a sliced fresh green chilli with the onion.

title: Beoseot jeongol (mushroom hot pot)
blurb: Mushrooms, napa cabbage and tofu arranged in sections in a wide pan, simmered in a clear soy dashi. Mild and quick.
intro: A jeongol is cooked and served in a wide, shallow pan on the table, so a steel sauté pan is the right tool here, not a substitute. Several kinds of mushroom sit in neat sections over napa cabbage and onion, with tofu and an optional mound of seasoned minced beef in the centre. A clear, lightly salted soy broth goes around the edge. It is mild, light and ready in half an hour. Use niboshi dashi or, for a vegetarian pot, shiitake-kombu dashi. This is a home adaptation built from several Korean sources and has not been kitchen tested.
equipment: Wide steel sauté pan with lid, 26–28 cm

mise.name: Base layer
mise.items: napa cabbage in 4 cm pieces · onion sliced lengthwise

mise.name: Mushrooms
mise.items: oyster torn into strips · shiitake caps scored · brown mushrooms halved · enoki in small bunches

mise.name: Seasoned beef
mise.items: minced beef mixed with soy, garlic, sesame oil, pepper

mise.name: Broth
mise.items: dashi · soy sauce · minced garlic · fish sauce

steps.title: Prepare the mushrooms
body: Wipe the mushrooms clean; do not soak them. Tear the oyster mushrooms along the gills into 1–2 cm strips.
Cut the stems off the shiitake and score a shallow cross into each cap. Halve the brown mushrooms. Cut the root block off the enoki and pull them into small bunches.

steps.title: Cut the vegetables; season the beef
body: Cut the napa cabbage into 4 cm pieces. Cut the ends off the onion, halve it and slice it lengthwise, along the lines, about 5 mm thick. Slice the carrot into thin rounds. Cut the tofu into 1 cm thick slices and the spring onions into 5 cm lengths.
If using beef, mix it with the soy sauce, 1 minced clove of garlic, sesame oil and pepper.
Stir the broth together: dashi, soy sauce, the other minced garlic clove and the fish sauce.

steps.title: Arrange the pan in sections
body: Spread the napa cabbage and onion over the bottom of the cold pan as a bed.

On top, arrange each mushroom in its own section around the pan, like the spokes of a wheel, with the tofu slices and carrot between them. Put the seasoned beef as a loose mound in the centre. Keep the enoki and spring onion aside.

steps.title: Pour the broth and simmer covered
body: Pour the broth gently down the side of the pan so the arrangement stays in place. It should come about halfway up the vegetables; the cabbage and mushrooms release more liquid as they cook.
Cover and bring to a boil on medium-high, then lower to medium and simmer for 6–8 minutes, until the cabbage is soft and the beef has turned brown.

steps.title: Add enoki and spring onion; eat from the pan
body: Uncover and break the beef mound into a few large pieces with a spoon. Lay in the enoki and spring onion and simmer for 1–2 minutes.
Taste the broth and add salt a pinch at a time; it should be lightly seasoned, like a soup. Bring the pan to the table and serve into small bowls with rice.

notes: Finish with noodles or rice
Korean meals often finish a jeongol by cooking something in the leftover broth. Add a portion of udon or a bowl of cooked rice, simmer for 2–3 minutes and stir in a beaten egg.
Any mushrooms work
Use at least three kinds for different textures: meaty (oyster, king oyster), firm (shiitake, brown) and delicate (enoki, shimeji). About 400–450 g of mushrooms in total suits 2 people.
A little warmth
For gentle heat, stir ½ tsp gochugaru into the broth, or add a sliced mild green chilli with the spring onion.

title: Galbi-jjim (braised beef short ribs)
blurb: Short ribs braised low and slow in soy, grated pear and garlic with radish, carrot and chestnuts until tender. Not spicy.
intro: A celebration dish: beef short ribs braised until they come away from the bone, in a sweet-savoury soy sauce softened with grated pear, with chunks of radish and carrot, shiitake and chestnuts. Completely mild. In Turkey ask for kaburga cut into 5 cm pieces. It works in a steel sauté pan with a tight-fitting lid (28 cm) on low heat. Turn the ribs a few times and keep some hot water nearby, because a wide pan loses more liquid than a pot. This is a home adaptation built from several Korean sources and has not been kitchen tested.
equipment: Wide steel sauté pan with tight lid, 28 cm
Tongs, ladle and small spoon for skimming
ingredients: ½ pear or 1 small apple (100 g)
600 ml, plus more to top up

mise.name: Braising sauce
mise.items: soy · sugar · honey · grated pear · grated onion · garlic · ginger · pepper · sesame oil

mise.name: Radish and carrot
mise.items: 4 cm chunks with the sharp edges trimmed round

mise.name: Shiitake, chestnuts, jujubes
mise.items: soaked shiitake caps halved · chestnuts · jujubes

steps.title: Soak and trim the ribs
body: Put the ribs in a large bowl of cold water for 30–60 minutes to draw out blood, changing the water once. Soak the dried shiitake in warm water at the same time.
Trim off thick outer pieces of fat. Make 2–3 shallow cuts along the meat of each rib so the sauce gets in.

steps.title: Blanch the ribs in the pan
body: Fill the sauté pan halfway with water and bring it to a boil. Add the drained ribs and boil for 5 minutes; grey scum will rise.
Drain the ribs into a colander and rinse each one under warm water. Wash out the pan. This makes the sauce clean and glossy instead of murky.

steps.title: Braise in the sauce, covered
body: Grate the pear and onion on the fine side of the grater and mince the garlic. Stir them into the soy sauce, sugar, honey, ginger, pepper and sesame oil.
Put the ribs back into the clean pan in one layer, pour over the sauce and the 600 ml water and bring to a boil. Cover, lower to low and braise at a gentle bubble for 1 hour.
Turn the ribs every 20 minutes. The liquid should stay at least halfway up the ribs; top up with hot water if it drops lower.

steps.title: Add radish, carrot, shiitake and chestnuts
body: Meanwhile, peel the radish and carrot and cut them into 4 cm chunks. Shave the sharp edges round with a small knife so they don't break up during the long braise. Squeeze the shiitake and halve the caps.
Tuck the radish, carrot, shiitake, chestnuts and jujubes between the ribs. Cover and braise on low for 30–40 minutes, until a chopstick slides easily into the meat and the radish is translucent.

steps.title: Skim and reduce to a glaze
body: Uncover the pan and tilt it slightly. Spoon off the clear fat that pools at the low side.

Raise the heat to medium and simmer uncovered for 8–10 minutes, spooning the sauce over the ribs, until it is thick and shiny and the ribs look lacquered. Move the vegetables gently so they don't break.

steps.title: Garnish and serve
body: Arrange the ribs and vegetables on a plate or serve from the pan. Spoon the remaining glaze over them, then scatter thinly sliced spring onion and sesame seeds. Eat with rice.

notes: Make it a day ahead

Galbi-jjim is even better the next day. Cool it and refrigerate it in the pan or a container. The next day, lift off the hardened fat and gently reheat it covered with a splash of water before reducing it to a glaze.
Pear is the tenderiser

Asian pear (nashi) has an enzyme that softens the meat and makes the sauce fruity. A crisp apple is the easiest substitute; kiwi works too but only use ¼ of one, because too much makes the meat mushy.
Lid fit matters

If your lid lets out a lot of steam, put a sheet of baking paper under it and check the liquid every 15 minutes. If you only have a loose lid, the slow part can be done in the oven at 160 °C in an oven-safe pan.

title: Budae jjigae (army stew)
blurb: Luncheon meat, sausages, kimchi, beans and ramen noodles simmered in a wide pan and topped with cheese. Mild version.
intro: Korea's post-war comfort stew: tinned luncheon meat, sausages and baked beans meet kimchi and instant noodles, with a slice of cheese melting on top. It is traditionally cooked in a wide, shallow pan in the middle of the table, so a steel sauté pan is ideal. The ingredients are arranged in sections, broth is poured around them and the noodles go in last. This version is mild: gochujang only, no chilli flakes. The heat comes from your kimchi, and you can control it. Beef luncheon meat and beef frankfurters (common in Turkey) work well. This is a home adaptation built from several Korean sources and has not been kitchen tested.
equipment: Wide steel sauté pan with lid, 28 cm

mise.name: Meats
mise.items: luncheon meat in 1 cm slices · frankfurters on the diagonal · minced beef

mise.name: Kimchi and vegetables
mise.items: kimchi chopped · onion sliced lengthwise · tofu slices · mushrooms

mise.name: Mild sauce
mise.items: gochujang · soy · garlic · mirin · sugar · pepper

mise.name: To finish
mise.items: ramen block · cheese slice · spring onion

steps.title: Slice and mix the sauce
body: Cut the luncheon meat into 1 cm thick slices and the frankfurters on the diagonal into 1 cm pieces. Chop the kimchi into bite-sized pieces.
Cut the ends off the onion, halve it and slice it lengthwise. Cut the tofu into 1 cm slices, the mushrooms into halves and the spring onions into 5 cm lengths.
Stir the gochujang, soy sauce, minced garlic, mirin, sugar and pepper into a thick paste. For a spicier pot, add the gochugaru.

steps.title: Arrange everything in the pan
body: Spread the onion over the bottom of the cold pan. On top, arrange the luncheon meat, frankfurters, kimchi, tofu and mushrooms in separate sections around the pan.
Spoon the baked beans and the minced beef into gaps. Put the sauce paste as one dollop in the centre.

steps.title: Pour in the stock and simmer
body: Pour the stock gently down the side of the pan until the ingredients are about two-thirds covered.

Cover and bring to a boil on medium-high, then cook for 5 minutes. Uncover, stir the sauce paste into the broth and break up the minced beef. Simmer for another 3 minutes and taste; add a splash of soy sauce if it needs more salt.

steps.title: Add noodles and cheese; eat right away
body: Put the ramen block in the centre and lay the cheese slice on top of it. Scatter the spring onions around.

Simmer for 2–3 minutes, loosening the noodles with chopsticks once they soften, until they are just cooked and the cheese has melted into the broth. Serve straight from the pan; the noodles keep softening.

notes: How spicy it gets
The sauce here has no chilli flakes, so the only heat comes from the kimchi. For a very mild pot, use less kimchi or squeeze out its juice. Classic budae jjigae uses 1–2 tbsp gochugaru.
What to use in Turkey

Pork Spam can be hard to find; tinned beef luncheon meat (dana jambon or dana luncheon) and beef frankfurters (dana sosis) taste close. Sucuk is too strongly spiced and greasy for this stew. Any baked beans in tomato sauce work.
Ramen

Use only the noodle block; keep the seasoning packet aside or add a quarter of it if the broth tastes flat. Korean ramyeon noodles hold up best, but any instant noodle works. Add more stock and a second block to stretch it for 4 people.
